newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH ATAG TO REORGANISE GERMAN UNITS.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH ATAG TO REORGANISE GERMAN UNITS.

text.p: Industrial group Atag Holding NV said on Friday it would further reorganise its German subsidiaries this year.
"We are going to take measures which, given the high wage costs in Germany, will enable us to improve our profitability," chief executieve Hans Manschot told a news conference.

Earlier, Atag said its 1996 net profit from ordinary operations had fallen by 37 percent to 16.5 million guilders. About half of the fall, which was in line with a previous forecast, was due to the difficult market situation in Germany and the other half to high introduction costs of new products.
Operating profit of Atag's home products division, which makes kitchen equipment and heaters, fell to 22.6 million guilders from 35.4 million in 1995.

The bicycle division raised its operating profit by 2.5 million guilders to 17.5 million in 1996, but German bicycles maker Hercules still made a loss despite a reorganisation in 1996 in which its number of workers was halved to about 160.

Therefore, making the German units healthier would be a top priority for Atag in 1997, Manschot said. These units generate 38 percent of the group's sales, which totalled 984.7 million guilders in 1996.
Hercules, which was bought in September 1995, will further reduce its number of employees and Atag's German home products subsidiary, which now employs 948 people, will also cut jobs.
Parts of the production of the German home products unit will probably be moved to Hungary, Manschot said.
He declined to give details about the number of jobs to be axed, adding Atag first had to negotiate with German trade unions and the subsidiaries' workers councils.
Manschot said Atag had previously built up a reorganisation provision of about 20 million guilders which is seen sufficient to cover the planned reorganisation costs.
The company, which was very active in buying other firms in recent years, does not plan any takeovers in the near future.
"At the moment we want to concentrate on reorganising our German companies in particular," Manschot said.
He added Atag plans to invest about 25 million guilders this year, mainly in the Netherlands and Hungary, which will be somewhat below the level of depreciations.
Manschot said the bulk of introduction costs for new products had now been taken and said the products, such as a new central heating boiler, had met a good market reception.
Although Atag expects introduction costs to be substantially lower this year, it does not want to give a profit forecast for 1997 given the uncertainty of the important German market.
Manschot said he did not expect the German market to show a recovery this year.
"I can see only very few positive signals there," he said.
